verification_candidates.claim_text: Antioxidant supplements have no evidence of any benefit.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: There's no evidence that they do anything
verification_candidates.rationale: The hosts assert an absence of evidence for a category of supplements, which can be checked against the literature.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Resveratrol is poorly absorbed, producing a blood spike of about 30 minutes before it is excreted or metabolized, so supplements cannot deliver a beneficial amount.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: you don't really absorb it, you get a spike of it for roughly 30 minutes
verification_candidates.rationale: The pharmacokinetic claim about resveratrol is checkable and central to the debunking.

verification_candidates.claim_text: The only real evidence that resveratrol has health effects comes from studies on yeast, fruit flies and mice.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: the only real evidence that resveratrol could be isolated and could have these health effects is on studies of yeast, fruit flies and mice
verification_candidates.rationale: A checkable characterization of the resveratrol evidence base, used to argue it does not support human benefit.

verification_candidates.claim_text: To get the dose of resveratrol given to mice, a person would have to drink 100 liters of wine.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: to get that amount of resveratrol, you'd have to drink 100 liters of wine
verification_candidates.rationale: A concrete dose-equivalence claim used to show the mouse study is irrelevant to humans.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Purple grape juice has an amazingly constant amount of resveratrol and contains more of the heart-protecting chemical than 60% of wines.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: grape juice had more of the heart protecting chemical than 60% of the wines he analyzed
verification_candidates.rationale: A quoted 1992 finding about resveratrol content in grape juice versus wine, used to undercut the wine-specific story.

verification_candidates.claim_text: A meta-analysis of alcohol and mortality found very good evidence that not drinking is the healthiest way to live and very good evidence that moderate drinking is the healthiest way to live.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: there is very good evidence that moderate drinking is the healthiest way to live
verification_candidates.rationale: The hosts report a meta-analytic finding about alcohol and mortality that is checkable and bears on the moderate-drinking debate.

verification_candidates.claim_text: French people have low heart attack rates.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: French people have low heart attack rates
verification_candidates.rationale: A population health statistic offered as the basis of the French paradox.
